query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A single compositional intervention that reduces density without compromising room‐temperature and ~1000 °C mechanical integrity is to partially substitute the heavy Hf component with a lightweight element such as Al. This substitution is expected to lower the overall alloy density while retaining a solid solution (or single BCC phase) that provides high strength at both ambient and elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³ and a predominantly BCC microstructure.
generation.intervention: Replace a fraction of Hf with Al (for example, a partial substitution on the Hf sublattice, e.g. 10–20 atomic percent replacement of Hf by Al), keeping the other elements unchanged.
generation.conditions: Casting conditions similar to the as‐cast alloy with testing over room temperature up to approximately 1000 °C under tensile and/or compressive loading, in order to verify mechanical integrity over this temperature range.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention is designed to maintain a predominantly BCC microstructure (or a similarly beneficial solid solution phase), where the light Al atoms enter the lattice, reducing the overall density without promoting deleterious phase separations. The retained phase is expected to provide solid solution strengthening, analogous to the as‐cast state.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum, being significantly lighter than Hf, will lower the alloy density when substituted. At the same time, because Al can contribute to solid solution strengthening (and in some cases can promote ordering in BCC high-entropy alloys), the mechanical performance at both room temperature and high temperature (~1000 °C) may be preserved if the substitution level is optimized to avoid over-stabilization of any brittle intermetallic phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is predicted to exhibit a reduction in overall density relative to 10.21 g/cm³ while retaining similar high strength and thermal stability as the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr at both room temperature and around 1000 °C. The directional change is a lower density without a significant loss in yield strength or creep resistance within the tested range.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr high-entropy alloy, which is known for its high strength but comparatively high density.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to conditions up to approximately 1000 °C and under mechanical loading regimes (e.g., tensile and compressive tests) similar to those used for evaluating the as-cast alloy’s performance.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal fraction of Hf substitution with Al that balances density reduction with phase stability and mechanical performance is not precisely known. Moreover, there is uncertainty regarding the potential for forming any deleterious secondary phases due to the addition of Al under the as-cast processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys with incremental substitution levels of Hf with Al (e.g., 0%, 10%, 20% replacement by atomic percentage). Process all samples under identical casting conditions to produce as-cast microstructures. Characterize the phase formation using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and microstructure by electron microscopy. Conduct density measurements, room temperature tensile tests, and high-temperature mechanical tests (around 1000 °C) to compare performance with the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
measurements: Room temperature yield strength and tensile ductility
High-temperature (∼1000 °C) yield strength and creep resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-substituted alloys do not show a significant decrease in overall density or if they exhibit a statistically significant deterioration (beyond experimental uncertainty) in mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength, ductility, or creep resistance) compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 (equiatomic atomic percentages). Processing: Vacuum arc melting (4 re-melts), casting into bars (gravity or suction-assisted), followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1230 °C and 152 MPa for 4 h. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests, compression tests at room temperature, and creep tests at 982 °C under 200 MPa and 120 MPa loads.
